en: Having fulfilled their purpose through the teaching of the unsurpassed *bodhicitta*, the Tathāgatas entreat for the sake of the Bodhisattvas. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then," and so forth: it is "essential" (*sāra*) because it is firm due to its single flavor with emptiness; it is "secret" (*rahasya*) because it is hidden; it is "mystery" (*guhya*) because it is not within the sphere of experience of those other than the Tathāgatas; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to *bodhicitta*; it is "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*) because, by not abiding in either cyclic existence or quiescence, there is nothing superior to it. This has been explained as the "heart of all tantras."

Knowledge itself is the lamp because it destroys the darkness of conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence; that very knowledge is the vajra because its single flavor is emptiness. Having entered the meditative absorption (samādhi) named after that, the meaning is: having stabilized the mind through the realization of the non-duality of wisdom and means, which are pure in all their aspects.

"Rahasya," and so forth. The meaning of the phrase "Thus have I [heard]" (*evam mayā*) and so on should be understood here as well. By the word *rahas* (secret), all the Tathāgatas are meant; that which exists therein, by virtue of its nature as the *dharmadhātu*, is the secret, namely the *dharmodayā*. He is situated there in the peaked pavilion atop Mount Sumeru. Alternatively, in the same way, it is the secret in the form of the consort’s womb (*bhaga*) embraced [by him]. Or again, in the same way, the secret refers to the wheels (*cakras*) such as the *nirmāṇa*-wheel, which are known as the wombs of the goddesses such as Locanā, whose intrinsic nature is earth and the other elements.

Alternatively, the "secret" (*rahasya*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the "fortune" (*bhaga*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). He dwelt abiding therein. To the question "In what kind of secret? he says: "Supreme" (*parama*). It is that in which there is the supreme, complete transcendental excellence (*lokottara-sampatti*) without remainder; or else, it is the object of supreme gnosis (*parama-jñāna*); or else, it is "supreme" because the ultimate (*paraṃ nirvāṇaṃ*)—in whatever way it may be—does not fit within or is not delimited by it.

Alternatively, it is "supreme" (*paramam*) because by means of it, enemies—the afflictions (*kleśa*)—are measured (*mīyante*) and marked (*lakṣma kriyante*) during the causal stage. It is the sphere for the arising of supreme bliss because it is delightful through the act of sporting in great bliss joined with the goddesses beginning with Locanā and ending with [Samayatārā]. Regarding "of the nature of all" (*sarvātmani*): it is the secret of all because it has the nature of all Tathāgatas; or alternatively, it is the nature of all because its essence consists of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the others; or alternatively, it is so because it has the nature of Vajradhara, who is everything. Thus it is.

By this, the perfection of place (*sthānasampad*) is explained. "Always abiding" means that he has not gone anywhere at any time, because the universe is identical with him. By virtue of being present, through the natural continuity of the flow [of existence], he is indicated here as abiding in this palace amidst an infinite inner court in the form of the *dharmakāya*, *sahajakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, in the twenty-first [chapter], beginning with "re" and so forth, the elements denoted by sixteen syllables are the Blessed One Vajradhara. However, in the twenty-fourth [chapter], by explaining the threefold meaning of the words beginning with "rahasya," the five Tathāgatas—the gnosis of the five elements—will be taught, and it will be stated that Vajrasattva has their nature as his own. All Buddhas, equal in number to the atoms of all world-realms, such as Śāśvata and the others, consist of all Buddhas because they have that as their nature and because they have that as their cause.

By this, the perfection of the assembly is described, because he is surrounded by all the Buddhas. He is a "being" (*sattva*) because he is intent upon performing purposeful activity for the sake of sentient beings—both directly and indirectly—for the lords of the ten stages and others. By this, the *saṃbhogakāya* is described. Vajrasattva is the nature of the *bodhicitta* inseparable from the *dharmakāya*, whose essence is emptiness, and the *sahajakāya*, whose essence is compassion and bliss; he consists of wisdom and means. Vajrasattva is the fourth body, the *sahajakāya*, whose nature is that supreme, untainted, and immutable great bliss.

[Objection: Is it not the case that since the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* is what is intended to be explained, why is anything else being said? [Response: It is not so; for the meaning is this: he who has just been described as one perfected in the welfare of self and others is himself the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.

Yoga is the union of emptiness and compassion; alternatively, it is called *yoga* because one is joined (*yojyate*) with the bliss of union with the goddesses. It is "firm" (*sthira*) because it is unshakable by the winds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It is "eternal" (*śāśvata*) because it persists until the furthest limit of the future. It is the "supreme Manmatha" because, through its unsurpassed passion, it churns the minds of all goddesses. It is "present" (*pratīty-utpanna*) in the sense that it exists as the intrinsic nature of each and every phenomenon (*sarvadharmāṇām svarūpatvena*); or alternatively, it is "arisen" (*utpanna*) in the sense of being currently manifest (*pratyutpanna*).

And because it is always beyond the past and the future, this nature—which consists of the *dharmakāya* devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvābhāvya*)—exists for all phenomena that abide in the three times. For it is stated in the *Dharmasaṃgītisūtra*: "Inconceivability exists conventionally; in the ultimate sense, the lack of intrinsic nature of phenomena is taught as the ultimate."

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), these [phenomena], being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), possess as their very essence the nature of being devoid of intrinsic nature; because this is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is insurmountable and cannot be transgressed—even by the Omniscient Ones, let alone by others. As it has been said in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi*:
"Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) remains constant—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."

And so forth. By this, the *dharmakāya* has been indicated. Desiring to explain the *nirmāṇakāya*, he says: "Diverse," and so forth. "Diverse" refers to action (*karman*), namely the practice of passion (*rāga*) and the like. "Diverse method" (*vidhi*) refers to the performance of the rites of Vajrasattva and others. For indeed, those whose conduct is characterized by passion and the like have a desire for the methods of Vajrasattva and others; for them, the Buddhas, Vajradharas, and so forth, are the antidotes to passion and the rest. The Buddha is Vairocana, the antidote to delusion (*moha*). Alternatively, "Buddha" refers to the Lord of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*), as it has been said: [source?]
On the tenth stage, a bodhisattva is to be called a Buddha, but not a *samyaksaṃbuddha*.

Vajradhara is the Vajra of the Thought of Enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). "Created" means having the nature of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). They are "disciplines" (*vinaya*) because they lead sentient beings to purity by removing the obstacles of afflictions and the knowable. "Remembered" means cultivated, not merely heard.

Alternatively, the meaning is that those who were remembered by the Blessed One while in the causal state (*hetvavasthā*)—thinking, "I shall discipline sentient beings through such various means of manifesting emanations"—are to be radiated forth without conceptualization while in the resultant state (*phalāvasthā*).

Thus, this Vajra of the Awakening Mind (*bodhicittavajra*), whose nature consists of the four bodies (*catuḥkāya*), becomes the intrinsic nature of all stable and moving phenomena, including all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth; for even stable things do not exist apart from one's own mind.

Who is this "thus" one? He says: "All," and so forth. All Buddhas are Vairocana and the others, whose nature consists of the mirror-like and other gnoses. Together with them, because he consists of the nectar of gnosis which has a single flavor with emptiness, he is in the form of all Buddhas. For him who has manifested for the sake of the world as Vajrasattva, there is a perfect union (*samyagyoga*)—that is, a meeting on the thirteenth stage, the Vajradhara level, which consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
And he is...

*Ḍā* means *ḍāḥ*. It is the act of traveling through space. From the word *ḍā*, the third case [instrumental] is applied. The root *ak* signifies moving in a crooked manner; here, "moving everywhere" constitutes that crooked movement. Thus, it means "she whose nature is to move (*akitum*) by means of *ḍā*. The meaning is that she goes everywhere simultaneously by means of her supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) through her manifold bodies. [This is the verse on Guṇavatī elsewhere.]
The inclusion of the term "vajra" is for the purpose of excluding the external ḍākinīs. They are both "vajras"—consisting of non-conceptual wisdom—and "ḍākinīs," thus they are *vajraḍākinīs*;
by implication, this refers to the *Guṇavatī*s. The intended meaning here is that the exclusion applies to all [such beings] everywhere.

Alternatively, she is called *ḍāyinī* because it is her nature (*śīla*) to bestow (*ḍātuṃ*) non-referential gnosis (*nirālambana-jñāna*) and to make it one's own. According to etymological interpretation (*nairukta*), when [these conditions] exist, she is a *ḍākinī*.

*Ḍākinī* is wisdom (*prajñā*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the "net" (*jāla*) is skillful means (*upāya*), which is compassion (*karuṇā*). From these two comes "bliss" (*śam*), the excellent (*varam*) and supreme (*utkṛṣṭam*) state, characterized by the excellences of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), greatness (*mahattva*), unsurpassedness (*niruttaratva*), and remaining for infinite time (*niravadhikālāvasthāyitva*). Because it excludes [one] from faults or because it covers [them], it is the *ḍākinījālasamvara* in the definitive sense (*nītārtha*).

In the sense of the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), however, through the union of all Buddhas (*sarvabuddhasamāyoga*)—that is, by the meeting of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth with Vairocana and the others—the *ḍākinīs* are, internally, either the nature of passion (*rajas*) or the channels (*nāḍī*). Their "net" (*jāla*) is their assembly. The Blessed One, whose essence is the seminal fluid (*śukra*), conceals that [net] through union, making it of a single flavor with unobscured great bliss; thus it is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.

Alternatively, through the union of all Buddhas—that is, by the meeting of Vairocana and the others within the maṇḍala circle—it is that whose "net" (*jāla*) is its illusory power (*māyā*), characterized by the manifestation of traveling through space in the ten directions. The *ḍākinīs* are those whose nature is to display such movement in the sky. (Rabhasakośa 305bc)
The term *jāla* refers to a net, a cluster, or a lattice-window; it is also said to mean a snare, a net, or deceit.

Just as there is an illusion (māyā) involving elephants and so forth, the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya display the illusory forms of Vajra goddesses like Gaurī in order to attract those disciples who are to be trained by women.

This, being both the *saṃvara* (the binding vow/discipline), is the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, which is Vajradhara himself in the nature of the Fruition Tantra (*phalatantra*), consisting of the four bodies (*kāyacatuṣṭaya*).

This indeed is the supreme fulfillment of one’s own welfare and the fulfillment of the welfare of others. Having previously mentioned—in the context of the word *sattva*—the state of being dependent on the fruit, which is unique [to the Buddha] directly, yet common [to others] indirectly, he now describes it primarily.

By means of such a person, they are led (*neyāḥ*) in every way, in all places and at all times, in various forms as appropriate; thus, "leading" (*vinayana*) is established, the rest being understood.

It is "universal" (*viśva*) because it manifests in infinite forms according to one's lineage (*gotra*) and the time when the latencies of merit (*puṇyavāsanā*) are awakened. It is "supreme" (*uttama*) because it demonstrates the most easily practiced means. It is "accomplished" (*siddha*) because it is perfected on the stage of a Buddha, functioning without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
or alternatively, it is "accomplished" (*siddha*) because it is eternal, functioning without interruption throughout the mental continua of limitless sentient beings.

It is "for the benefit of all beings" (*sarvasattvārtha*) because the welfare of all beings proceeds from it. This is because it brings about the attainment of the supreme human goal—non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), which is the object to be sought and accomplished—for ordinary beings with weak, medium, and sharp faculties, as well as for those beings who are somewhat purified, namely the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. For this very reason, it is "supreme. Furthermore, it is supreme because, through the intentional teaching of the three vehicles (*yāna-traya*), it reveals that the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*) alone is the ultimate goal.

Alternatively, "universal" (*viśva*) is so called because it consists of the three forms of the good rebirths and liberation; "supreme" (*uttama*) because it is established as superior to the liberations taught by others, and because, by way of implication, the welfare of all sentient beings is accomplished as supreme, since even the good rebirths and so forth ultimately culminate in perfect enlightenment. In these [words], the neuter gender is used for the sake of the meaning.

Now, for the sake of accomplishing the aforementioned Vajrasattva, he explains the primary *upāyatantra* (means-tantra), beginning with the words "all" (*sarva*) and so forth. All women—whether they are established as illusory by nature through transformations in which their own form, which is the basis of obscurations, has its obscurations rendered subtle in some cases, or is entirely free from obscurations in others—become accomplished yoginīs, Vajrayoginīs, through service; they become bestowers of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā for the practitioner.

Those whose nature it is to act among the wicked and the unwholesome also achieve success by being intent upon the practice of the wholesome through abstention from the unwholesome. How so? It is obtained through all [means], such as the enjoyment of objects like forms as they happen to be encountered, embracing, kissing, and the entry of the vajra, and so forth.
And that bliss which is the attainment of everything is the innate (*sahaja*); its "festivals" are the successive, continuous arisings, and by means of those material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

And he says that all those women should be visualized as having the nature of the deities of the two feet: "Vicitrā" refers to Vajravārāhī and others in their various forms; though they are illusory and ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), they appear conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*). "Mudrā" is according to the etymology to be explained later. She herself is the *ḍākinī*. How so? By means of the "mleccha" [term] to be explained, which is the Blessed One’s secret code (*saṃketa*). For instance: *ḍai* and so forth. Moving through the air is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Therefore he says: "The entire sky is the selflessness (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of all phenomena. She moves within that and becomes one with it; thus she is the 'Sky-Walker' (*sarvākāśacarā*). She is "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) because she is accomplished by means of this [practice]; she is the *ḍākinī* because her essential nature is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Thus, when it is said "among women," this [ḍākinī] is to be visualized through identification (*tādātmyena*). In some places, the reading is *iti*; in that case, *iti* means that by means of her, one goes toward or approaches attachment to entities and so forth.

He explains what was indicated by the term "mudrā": "from all sides" means from all ten directions; it "seals" (mudrayati) the universe—consisting of the aggregates and so forth—or it "bestows joy" (mudaṃ rāti).
Thus, the "seal of the universe" is *viśvamudrā*.
How [is this so]? Because, through the emptiness that is utterly pure, one enjoys objects such as forms from all sides with various, all-pervading natures—pleasures that are excellent and supreme.
Thus, these families belong to those goddesses, such as Locanā, whose natures are characterized by such resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
"Vajra" refers to Akṣobhya, whose essence is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).
Vajradhara is Vajrasattva.
Like a lotus (*padma*), [he is] Vairocana, because he is unafflicted by the defects of cyclic existence, just as a lotus is unafflicted by the defects of water.
Here, the metaphorical designation for all the Tathāgatas, intended to indicate their state of being free from obscurations, is primarily illustrative; Padmadhara is Amitābha.
From the application of the *maṇi*, Ratnasambhava is the *maṇi*;
Amoghasiddhi is the bearer of the *maṇi*, because he holds the *khaḍgaratna* (sword-jewel) of the *maṇi*.
The intended meaning is that the yogin achieves success by manifesting himself in the form of any one of the [deities] such as Vajradhara, together with his own retinue of ḍākinīs.
Thus, they say that by this, the *jñānamudrā* is also indicated.

Having thus explained the *upāyatantra*, he now shows the *hetutantra*, which is the unsurpassed cause, namely the *bodhicitta*. The word "atha" (now) means immediately after the elucidation of the *upāya*.
That [tantra] in which all external and internal things, along with the subtle latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obscurations, are overcome and rendered empty within the five aggregates.

For this very reason, it is "dustless" (*viraja*) because it is free from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), since the term *rajas* is said to mean "dust. And the "state" (*pada*)—the perfection of the welfare of oneself and others, the locus of the ultimate goal—he entered into that samādhi and taught the *bodhicitta*, which is devoid of the grasping at subject and object and so forth, whose single flavor is emptiness, which is inseparable [from it], and which consists of body, speech, and mind.

The meaning is that he has described the essential nature of the Causal Vajradhara, who is the supreme state of union with Mahāmudrā for one who has entered that very samādhi. It is not empty in the sense of being a total negation (*apavāda*), because it appears conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*). It is not non-empty from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatvāt*). Nor is it ultimately real in the form of luminosity; yet it is not non-existent either, because it is perceived by others through its qualities such as being an object of cognition. Thus, the world is found to be the Middle Way.

For its proof is apprehension; and since that self-cognition is not a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is an absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*). Furthermore, there is a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*):
"Just as a form in a mirror is devoid of being either one or different [from it]," as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
And yet it is not found there; likewise is the nature of things within the realms of existence.

The sense is that this has been revealed many times in the Sūtras and other scriptures by such statements as these. Thus, the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatātattva*) has been illuminated by the first half [of the verse]. Nor is that alone the causal tantra (*hetutantra*), for the union (*yoga*)—that is, the identity (*tādātmya*)—with emptiness, which is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), is the means (*upāya*) and the cause of the resultant Vajradhara. The reading *karuṇātmanaḥ* (of the one whose nature is compassion) occurs in some versions.

Since this is so, great compassion (*mahākṛpā*), which has great mercy as its objective support, is the means; because of the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) with it, that very Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the "radiance"—the connection being that it is the *bodhicitta* appearing as conventional reality.
By this, it is stated that the world itself, whose nature consists of emptiness and compassion that are without beginning or end, is the unsurpassed cause of the *bodhicitta*.

He indicates the means for its realization—meditation—which will be explained in the sixth [chapter], with the words "in the non-conceptual": regarding all phenomena, such as the five aggregates of form and so forth, which are free from all superimpositions, there is no entity (*bhāva*) to be meditated upon as an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because all phenomena are empty. Nor is there a meditator, because of the absence of anything to be meditated upon. The intention is that the very non-conceptualization of all phenomena is itself meditation. As he will say: "Where there is no meditator whatsoever, nor any meditation, and nothing at all to be meditated upon—that is called the meditation on reality."

[Objection: If there is no conceptualization (*avikalpana*), how can there be the accomplishment of the service of the pledges (*samayasevā*) and so forth, or the specific stages of one’s own realization, or the welfare of others? [Response: He says "without" (*ava-*) and so on.

Even while there is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in non-conceptuality, the yogin should effect the accomplishment of all the conceptualizations of the service of the pledges and so forth. Being primarily characterized by resolute conviction in non-conceptuality, he further applies himself to the welfare of sentient beings, having anticipated the possibility of turning away from the welfare of others.

"Regarding 'in the non-conceptual' and so forth: thus, in this stage of initial practice, non-conceptualization occurs through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) alone; and therein, it is intended that one accomplishes everything.

However, when, through the progressive culmination of cultivation, the *bodhicitta*—which has the nature of all Tathāgatas—becomes the Dharma, namely the *dharmakāya*, then there is no longer a substratum (*dharmin*), because the aggregates of form and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Nor is its very nature (*dharmatā*) merely its property (*dharma*), for it is emptiness."
Conventionally, however, both are established as being non-different, because emptiness is not separate from phenomena. Thus it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*:
"Having become one whose intention is free from conceptual construction, O Son of the Conqueror, regarding this true Dharma..."
Having gradually transcended the fortress of conceptual construction, one attains the state free from conceptualization.
Tranquil, immovable, supreme, powerful, equal to the unequaled—
therefore, the bodhisattva attains the bliss of non-conceptuality.

Thus, here the non-conceptual resolve (*avikalpādhimokṣa*), which relies on the absence of conceptualization regarding the true reality (*tattva*) of the sublime Dharma, is firm. Conceptualization itself is fourfold and difficult to traverse; it is the sequence of practice. One attains non-conceptual, non-proliferated knowledge (*niṣprapañcajñāna*). From that knowledge, one attains bliss: it is tranquil because it is free from afflictions (*niḥkleśatva*); it is immovable because it is not subject to decline; and it is supreme because it excels all worldly and supramundane bliss.

It is powerful because it can be manifested at will, as much as one desires; it is equal to other pleasures by way of its class of pleasure (*sukhajāti*); yet it is unequal to those [other pleasures] by virtue of these four specific qualities. Thus, with the words "in the absence of conceptual constructions" (*avikalpeṣu*) and so forth, the disappearance of all conceptual constructions such as meditation on the part of the Vajradhara who possesses the fruit is indicated. Even so, through the sovereign power of his previous vows, he proceeds to benefit others without limit; therefore, it says "from that Vajradhara. It is like the sound of an echo.

Because of the equality [of all phenomena] through their lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*) and their freedom from the conceptual constructions that give rise to them, the Mahāyāna—consisting of the *Hetutantra* and so forth, as well as the *Vāk-sampuṭatantra* and so forth—is the Dharma itself realized by oneself. Thus, the unsurpassed *bodhicitta*, which is the fruit and the basis for the excellence of the fulfillment of the welfare of others, is called "bodhicitta" by way of incidental context; with the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) that the cause itself, when purified, is the fruit.

In this regard, in order to demonstrate his faith through realization (*avetyaprasāda*) toward the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana, he says "Then," and so forth. Because he is endowed with the accomplishment of the welfare of others through the perfection of cause and fruit, they praised that Vajradhara. That which is attained or reached is the primary "vehicle" (*yāna*), namely the fruit; whereas that by which one goes is the secondary "vehicle," namely the path. Furthermore, the composition of the text denotes both of these.

Because it possesses the ninefold greatness as explained in the *Munimatālaṃkāra* compared to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and others, and because that vehicle is great, it is the Mahāyāna. In this context, "those whose perfect manifestation" refers to the qualities about to be described; "by their expansions" means by their extensive developments. The "three times" are the three periods of time; those existing within them are "belonging to the three times" (*traiyadhvika*). Among these, those whose activities such as teaching have ceased in the world-system are established as "past."

Those who teach with the underlying intention that [these teachings] are like non-existents because they accomplish nothing even for a sentient being are those of the present. Those who will teach them are those of the future. Yet all of them exist; this same arrangement holds even in other world-systems.

Yoga is the nature of bodhicitta; through mastery therein, he is the Lord of Yoga (yogādhipa). Having thus stated the praise for the perfection of his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*), he speaks of the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*) with the words "liberator of beings" (*sattvamocaka*). He also speaks [of this] by way of being composed of the five Tathāgatas. Regarding the term "born as the self of all" (*sarvātmaja*): Vajrasattva is "born as the self of all" because he is born from the self (*ātman*), which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), of all [the Buddhas] such as Vairocana and the rest. He explains this very state of being the self of all with the words "having a single nature" (*ekabhāvaka*), and so forth.

Ratnasambhava is the "single-natured one" (*ekabhāvaka*), because through the nature of the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), he experiences the entire universe as having a single flavor. Vairocana is the "severer of delusion," because through the nature of the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*), he cuts through ignorance. Amoghasiddhi is "all-encompassing," because through the nature of the knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), he effects the welfare of all;
as it is said: "The All resides within the Self of the All. (Hevajratantra I.v.13d = Saṃpuṭa).

Because one contemplates the world as non-conceptual great bliss through the nature of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), the reality (*tattva*) here is Amitābha. As it is said in the *Hevajratantra* (I.v.14):
"Reality is by virtue of its being true bliss."

Because its nature is the wisdom of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*, this wisdom is Akṣobhya. Thus, the single Leader, whose essence is the five Tathāgatas, is the Blessed One Bodhicittavajra; he is the "Revealer" because, in accordance with those to be trained (*vineya*), he manifests in the forms of Akṣobhya and the others.
"I" refers to the one Tathāgata. In this way, all [the Tathāgatas] pay homage individually. For this very reason, the compiler used the plural form, saying "they praise."

Wishing to demonstrate the pervasiveness of the *hetu-tantra*, they make this request; thus he says "Furthermore," and so forth. "Essence" (*sāra*) refers to the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). That in which there is the single, non-dual self-nature—the inclusion or internalization—of all phenomena is called "the single inclusion of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmaikasaṃgraha*).

The sense faculties are those beginning with the eye; their state of being a path or an object extends as far as whatever thing whatsoever may be seen, heard, smelled, touched, or thought—that each of these is individually "in meditative equipoise" (*samāhita*) is the connection [of the sentence]. By way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that is, by its own essence or primordial nature (*prakṛti*). For the *dharmadhātu*, which is without beginning or end, is the primordial nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāṇām prakṛtiḥ*). How so? Through the yoga of non-equipoise (*asamāhitayogena*).

The meaning is: through the resolve (*adhimokṣa*)—which is yoga—that consists in the conviction that the objects of sight and so forth, appearing in vision and so on, are in their very nature Vajrasattva; [this resolve] is directed toward the peerless, supramundane, non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*) bodhicitta called Vajradhara, which is likewise beneficial, both in its state of non-equipoise (*asamāhita*) and its equipoise (*samāhita*). It is "placed" (*āhita*)—that is, maintained through identity—within that bodhicitta, which is equal in both the impure and pure states and is indivisible from emptiness and compassion.
By this, it is stated that [the nature] pervades both form and so forth, as well as the states of the impure and pure mind. For this very reason, it is said in the *Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭatantra*:
"Whatever sense-faculty may proceed along its path, each of those is by its own nature [that very nature]."
"By the enjoyment of all desires, one should carry everything as being composed of the Buddha.

If [the mind] is naturally in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), then what is the use of an equipoised resolve (*asamāhitādhimokṣa*)? Because they awaken [to it]. The word "aggregate" (*skandha*) is used in the singular to denote the class. Since there is no other self (*ātman*), the self whose nature consists of the five aggregates is based upon a distinguished knowledge—namely, consciousness (*vijñāna*) or the *bodhicitta*—in its entirety through the identity of the conventional and the ultimate; thus, they do not perceive it through direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). "Those who are deluded" refers to the lowest of men, such as the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), who possess deluded minds.

For they, being deluded regarding the very thought of awakening (bodhicitta), conceptualize such things as "that which thinks" (cettā) and so forth. Regarding that, the proponents of Īśvara [say] that the thinker is the eternal or non-eternal knowledge, namely the Person (puruṣa) or the Lord (īśvara)—the reading here is *cetiti*. The meaning is that he accumulates or heaps together the auspicious and inauspicious. The proponents of Sattva [say] it is the sentient being (*sattva*); the Sāṃkhyas [say] it is the Person whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*); the followers of the Upaniṣads [say] it is all-consciousness (*vijñāna*); and those who hold to the self (*ātman*) and so forth [say] it is that which has the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeyasvarūpaka*).

In this regard, the proponents of the Self (*ātmavādinaḥ*) maintain that it is the Self alone which, as if being a sentient being (*sattva*), is born, ages, dies, is bound, and is liberated. Likewise, the Digambaras [maintain] it is the "living soul" (*jīva*). The proponents of Time (*kālavādinaḥ*) hold that time creates beings and time destroys creatures. Furthermore, it is called a "person" (*pudgala*) because of its repeated dissolution into the various states of existence; or else, it is called a "person" because it is filled (*pūryate*) by karmas and decays (*kulati*) through their very exhaustion—thus say the proponents of the Person (*pudgalavādinaḥ*). This refers to [their view on] causality.

Only the proponents of Īśvara [theists] hold that the Lord alone is the cause of the entire aggregate of effects. Regarding the phrase "cultivation of the substratum" (*dharmibhāvanā*): it is precisely those who follow the Śaiva Siddhānta who maintain that the Lord is the instigator of merit and so forth. By this, it is shown that the object regarding which these [opponents] have a delusion concerning what is not their own tenet (*apasiddhānta*) is indeed the reality (*tattva*). How is there a delusion? Because, due to the multiplicity of attributes such as *cittā* and the rest, the multiplicity of the reality (*tattva*) would not be logically consistent; thus, [the opponent's position] is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

But the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that "the lowest of men" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). For because of the superimposition of the unreal (*abhūtasamāropa*) by ignorance (*avidyā*), which has existed throughout beginningless existence, reality (*tattva*) does not become manifest as it truly is; therefore, it is appropriate for ordinary worldlings to have resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) for the sake of perceiving that [reality]. They do not merely fail to realize the self, but also [fail to realize] the cognizer and so forth, [thinking] "this is consciousness. Thus, the summary of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is repeated:
that very same meaning is again presented by relying on a different formulation.

Furthermore, according to the *Nyāya*, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is explained as follows: "mind" (*citta*) refers to the complex of the eye and other [senses]; "that which knows" (*tajjñāna*) is the mind; and "it is cognized by the mind" (*cittena rūpyate*)—thus, form (*rūpa*) such as blue and so forth, which has the nature of cognition (*cidrūpa*), is the "seeing" (*darśana*); this is the [meaning of the] element (*dhātu*). In this way, the eighteen elements have the nature of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). And that object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is its own essential nature (*svarūpaka*). It is the ultimate emptiness (*pāramārthika-śūnyatā*) which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that essential form which is to be known and directly realized by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The sense is that one becomes resolved (*adhimucyate*) upon that.

If this is so, then through the cultivation of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), both the causal relationship and the emptiness of the phenomena (*dharma*) such as form (*rūpa*)—which are the subjects (*dharmin*)—are made manifest. One should cultivate with intent the relationship between property and subject (*dharmadharmibhāva*). [An objection: In that case, the relationship between property and subject would be something other than the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and thus it would not pervade it. To this he says: "In the effects" (*kāryeṣu*). This refers to the successive realizations. Properties (*dharma*) are such as the absence of intrinsic nature, momentariness, and being devoid of the grasped and the grasper; the cultivation of these within their respective subjects is the "cultivation of the properties" (*dharmabhāvanā*).

Whatever causes there may be, whatever effects there may be, and whatever phenomena (*dharma*) or substrata of phenomena (*dharmin*) there may be—their very nature consists solely of the essence of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); thus, emptiness is all-pervasive. Now, one might object: since the substrata (*dharmin*) are distinct from one another, how can their property (*dharma*)—namely, the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*)—be pervasive? For if, in the ultimate sense, that property is not distinct from the nature of the substratum, then with each difference in the substratum, how could it possess pervasiveness? To this he says: "Because," and so forth. Because phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are manifold; yet, despite this multiplicity and distinction, no multiplicity or distinction is perceived in the reality (*tattva*) that depends upon them.

Just as the many currents of rivers, though they pervade the ocean which contains them within itself, do not constitute a multiplicity for that lord of rivers; [here] "river-current" (*nadīsrotas*) is the singular used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*) with the meaning of a genitive case. The connection is: "by the multiplicity of river-currents. Why is there no such understanding? Because (*hi*), that which liberates—expressed by the suffix *-ac*—is liberation, namely the *bodhicitta*, which as the causal tantra (*hetutantra*) is indeed one alone.

This has been stated: emptiness alone is the reality (*tattva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*). And that, being of the nature of the exclusion of all superimpositions (*samāropa*), is designated as one, because it exists through its identity with each individual thing by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). However, it is not ultimately one like the universals (*sāmānya*) imagined by others. For it has been said that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there are neither phenomena nor a nature of phenomena distinct from or non-distinct from them.

Because its essence is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the knowledge of emptiness is also called reality (*tattva*) in the same way as emptiness itself; that very [knowledge] is the *bodhicitta*, and therefore it too is all-pervasive. And it was said previously: "The entire world, including the stationary and the moving, is pervaded by the Pervader. Furthermore, this very form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), when cultivated, produces the fruit of liberation consisting of great bliss. For there is indeed a similarity of kind between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*). Thus, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭkoṭīṭīkā*: [Q/R *Pradīpoddyotana* (see Chakravarti 1984: 74)]

Because of being a vajra-body, through union with immeasurable goddesses, until the end of saṃsāra, one experiences the bliss of the eightfold sovereignty that transcends gods, humans, and others, in a single moment of supreme joy (*paramānanda*); this is liberation—such is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

As for great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the gurus will explain how and by what means it remains, having cast off the self’s conceptualizations through various methods such as the *caṇḍālī*. Having explained the words to be spoken, he will say: "This very internal distinction is obtained from the mouth of the guru with extreme clarity."
That by which the teaching of reality (*tattva*) is presented through a detailed and extensive exposition is the *Tattvodeśa* chapter.
The third cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*.
